verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse calls the revealed Qur’anic verses exalted signs of the Book. “The Book” primarily means the Qur’an; its indefinite description and the distant demonstrative “these” both emphasize its grandeur and high rank. The manifest Qur’an is one of great significance that distinguishes truth from falsehood, refuting the disbelievers’ charge that the Prophet is mad and that God’s words are mockery.

It is also possible that “the Book” means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), from which the Qur’an originates, as indicated by “This is indeed a noble Qur’an in a guarded Book” (al-Waqi’ah:77-78) and “Indeed it is a glorious Quran, in a preserved tablet” (al-Burūj:21-22). Thus, the phrase summarizes: “By the manifest Book: We have made it into an Arabic Qur’an so that you may apply reason” (al-Zukhrūf:1-3).
verses.2: Al-Mizan explains that the verse foretells the disbelievers’ regret over their disbelief when worldly life ends: they will long to have been Muslims, devoted to God and believing in His Book, when attaining Islam is no longer possible. “Wish” denotes longing rather than mere liking, and “that they had been Muslims” shows that they will desire a past condition they have missed and cannot return to. It also precedes their later address to the Prophet, “O you, to whom the reminder has been sent down, you are indeed crazy” (15:6).
verses.3: Al-Mizan explains ‘diversion’ as being so engrossed in one thing that one neglects another. “Leave them to eat and enjoy and to be diverted” commands that the disbelievers be left in their falsehood, without debate or proofs, for they will soon know the truth and regret not having been Muslims when repentance is too late. Their concern is eating, worldly pleasure, and fleeting hopes, a mode of reasoning likened to that of beasts and speechless creatures; thus one should keep apart from them and not offer them arguments founded on sound intellect and human reasoning.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that these verses confirm “Soon they will know”: the disbelievers will not accept Islam in worldly life, but will wish to do so only after their appointed term has ended and doom has come. Every community has with God a known record fixing its lifespan, which it cannot advance or defer even by a moment; thus, nations, like individuals, have a designated record.

verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that, departing from a merely mocking tone, they addressed the Prophet by the claimed characteristic that the Reminder had been sent down to him rather than by name. The passive wording betrays their ignorance of its source and their disbelief in his claim that God revealed it. Both “to whom the Reminder has been sent down” and “Reminder” are mocking expressions, while calling him crazy seeks to discredit his claim. The editor notes that this wording may also suggest some hesitation or uncertainty about the revelation’s source, making their speech less than straightforward mockery.
verses.7: Al-Mizan explains that “why do you not” (law mā), like “why wouldn’t you” (hallā), is a provocative challenge: if the Prophet’s claim to prophethood is true, he should bring angels as witnesses, as in “Why has an angel not been sent down to him so that he may be a warner with him” (al-Furqan:7). The idolaters regarded human beings as material creatures subject to lust and anger and could not conceive a connection between humanity and the celestial realm of pure light and purity; therefore, they demanded that one claiming such a connection produce its inhabitants, the angels, to confirm him. Since they considered angels subordinate deities, the monotheistic claim also denied them any independent role in intercession or worship except by God’s permission. Their demand consequently implied that the angels should descend to validate the prophetic call.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse answers the demand that the Prophet produce angels to prove his truthfulness. Angels ordinarily remain concealed in the Unseen; if they descended at the disbelievers’ own demand as an extraordinary and decisive sign, their descent would be with a truth that admits no doubt. If they then disbelieved, no respite would remain and immediate destruction would follow.

The commentary reports three interpretations of “with due reason”: that the angels descend with punishment and eradication; that they descend with death, after which there is no delay, as in “The day when they see the angels, there will be no good news for the guilty that day” (al-Furqān:22); or that they descend only with the divine message and revelation. Yet none properly accords with the unrestricted wording, since angelic descent cannot be confined exclusively to punishment, death, or revelation.

Al-Mizan proposes that the verse may be understood through the difference between this material world and the angelic realm. Worldly life combines truth and falsehood, so truth does not appear here with all its properties and consequences; it remains liable to ambiguity and doubt. This mixture makes life a trial, allowing people to distinguish good from evil by their signs and results and to choose the path of happiness or misery. Even if a messenger had been made an angel, he would have been made to appear as a man and would therefore still have been subject to their confusion: “Had We made him an angel, We would have surely made him a man, and We would have surely confounded them just as they confound (the truth now)” (al-An’ām:9).

Angels, by contrast, belong to a realm of pure truth, free of falsehood, deficiency, evil, misery, corruption, and disobedience. They “do not disobey whatever Allah has commanded them, and carry out what they are commanded” (al-Taḥrīm:6), and “do not venture to speak ahead of Him, and they act by His command” (al-Anbiyā’:26-27). The conditions of material life—choice, probability, obedience and defiance, joy and sorrow—therefore do not apply to them.

As long as people are immersed in this worldly condition, like the disbelievers and the astray, they cannot reach the realm of pure truth. They attain it only by passing from this life to the Hereafter, when the veil is removed and sight becomes acute, as indicated by “You were certainly oblivious of this. We have removed your veil from you, and so your sight is acute today” (Qaf:22). Thus, for ordinary people, seeing angels in their true form is contingent on death. God’s chosen and purified servants, especially the Prophets (peace be upon them), are exceptions: being free from the stain of sin and near to God, they can perceive the Unseen while still in this world.

The commentary therefore suggests that the demand to see angels in their true forms was effectively a demand for the condition in which such sight becomes possible: death and the ensuing encounter with pure truth. This accords with “Those who do not expect to encounter Us say, ‘Why have angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?’ Certainly they are full of arrogance within their souls and have become terribly defiant. The day when they see the angels, there will be no good news for the guilty that day, and they will say, ‘Keep away (from paradise)!’ Then we shall attend to the works they have done and then turn them into scattered dust” (al-Furqān:21-23).

This also yields the verse’s dual implication. Sending angels as conclusive signs of prophethood would bring divine judgment and remove respite; sending an angel as a prophet would require making him appear human, leaving room for doubt. Divine testing requires the real possibility of success or failure, salvation or doom.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse’s emphatic wording answers those who dismissed the Qur’an as delusion and called the Prophet mad, while demanding angels to authenticate his claim. The meaning, God knows best, is that the Reminder was not devised by the Prophet, cannot be overcome by opponents’ obstinacy, does not depend on angels’ confirmation, and is not entrusted to the Prophet for preservation. God Himself gradually sent it down and preserves it because it is the Reminder.

The Reminder, namely the Qur’an, is living and enduring: it is protected from extinction and oblivion, from additions or omissions that would impair its reality as a Reminder, and from changes in wording or arrangement that would alter its function of disclosing the realities of divine wisdom. Thus the Book remains wholly preserved as an everlasting Reminder. This agrees with: “Indeed those who defy the Reminder when it comes to them. Indeed it is an august Book: falsehood cannot approach it, from before it nor from behind it, (gradually) sent down (revelation) from One all-wise, all-laudable” (Fussilat:41-42).

The definite article in al-dhikr denotes the particular covenantal Reminder, and “We will preserve it” conveys God’s receiving and preserving it after its revelation. This answers the objection that the Torah and Gospel, also called reminders, would consequently have the same immunity despite the Qur’an’s acknowledgment of distortions in them. In this context, the Reminder specifically means the Qur’an revealed to the Prophet and preserved thereafter; the verse concerns its content and significance, not an independent claim of superiority in divine protection.

In Tafsīr al-Qummī, Imām al-Ṣādiq is reported to have said that on the Day of Resurrection a caller from God’s side will announce that only a Muslim enters Paradise; then the disbelievers will wish that they had been Muslims, and he recited “Leave them to eat and enjoy and to be diverted by longings (by their activities). Soon they will know” (15:3). Al-ʿAyyāshī reportedly relates a similar interpretation from Imām al-Bāqir and Imām al-Ṣādiq through ʿAṭāʾ al-Makkī.

Al-Durr al-manthūr reports with a sound chain from Jābir b. ‘Abd Allah that the Messenger of God said that members of his community may be punished in Hellfire for their sins as long as God wills. Though the polytheists mock their faith, God will eventually remove every believer from the Fire; the Prophet then recited that the faithless will wish they had been Muslims. The same meaning is reported in various forms from Abū Mūsā al-Ashaʿrī, Abū Saʿīd al-Khuḍrī, and Anas b. Mālik.

A report attributed through ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib to the Messenger of God states that unrepentant monotheists guilty of major sins may enter Hell according to their deeds, but their monotheism and prostration protect them from eternal damnation and several of its humiliating punishments. Their punishment varies in degree and duration; when God removes them, followers of other religions in Hell object that the monotheists had believed in God, His Books, and His messengers yet shared their punishment. God then transfers the monotheists to a spring, where they grow as plants grow in a torrent’s residue, and admits them to Paradise. They enter bearing the inscription that they were inmates of Hell freed by the Merciful, then ask for it to be erased, which God grants; those left in Hell are sealed there and forgotten beside the Throne. The report identifies this as the meaning of the faithless wishing they had been Muslims. The commentary explains that al-Tarthūth is a plant and ḥamīl al-sayl its residue borne by a torrent, and notes similar Shiite reports.

Al-Durr al-manthūr also reports from Abū Saʿīd al-Khuḍrī that the Messenger of God set three sticks before, beside, and behind himself: the first represented man, the adjacent stick his lifespan, and the one behind his hopes. Man pursues his hopes, but his lifespan overtakes him before he reaches them. The commentary says a similar report comes through Anas. Majma’ al-bayyān reports from Amīr al-Muʾminīn that the two gravest things feared for people are following desire, which bars them from truth, and long hope, which makes them forget the Hereafter. Tafsīr al-Qummī interprets “We do not send down the angels except in truth, and they would not be given any respite” to mean that, if the angels were sent down, the people would receive no respite and would be destroyed.

Al-Mizan then examines the Qur’an’s immunity to distortion. Historically, the Qur’an now possessed is the very Book the Prophet brought and recited; it was not replaced by another book later attributed to him. Even those who have alleged distortion do not claim such wholesale replacement, but speak only of possible additions, omissions, changes of words, diacritics, or sequence. The Qur’an presently in people’s hands displays throughout the qualities it claims for itself: unsurpassed eloquence, harmony without genuine contradiction, a decisive and truthful account of knowledge, moral virtue, and monotheism, narratives that preserve the dignity of the prophets, fulfilled foretellings, and comprehensive guidance as light and a guide. Its verses explain one another where difficulty appears.

Most comprehensively, it is dhikr, God’s enduring reminder: it discloses His names, attributes, creation, angels, scriptures, messengers, decrees, resurrection, return to Him, and the ultimate success or misery of souls. Falsehood entering it through refutation, replacement, alteration, or distortion would negate this character. The commentary therefore rejects the claim that the pronoun in “indeed We will preserve it” refers to the Prophet: the context concerns the Qur’an for which the disbelievers mocked him, as in “They said, ‘O you, to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are indeed crazy’” (15:6). The Qur’an revealed to the Prophet is thus protected from additions, subtractions, and alterations that would affect its attributes. If one supposes some omission or minute change, such as a repeated verse or a dot or inflection, it must be one that does not impair its inimitability, guidance, luminosity, superiority to other scriptures, or nature as dhikr.

Numerous reports transmitted through both Shīʿah and Sunnī channels instruct believers to return to the Qur’an in confusion and to judge reports by it. The Ḥadīth al-Thaqalayn—“the Book of God and my progeny, my Ahl al-Bayt”—would not direct people to a distorted book incapable of preventing misguidance. Comparing reports with the Qur’an is not restricted to jurisprudence: fabricated material also entered reports about belief, prophets, creation, and the end, especially al-Isrāʾīlīyāt. The Imāms’ citations on varied subjects correspond to the Qur’an now held by Muslims, even in reports alleged to concern distortion; many such reports instead distinguish explanatory narration from the revealed text. Reports from the Imāms also tell their Shīʿah, “Recite the Qur’an as the people do.” Hence differences between the present text and Imām ʿAlī’s compilation, if any, concern the ordering of sūrahs or verses rather than the divine meanings and attributes of the revelation.

Some hadith scholars among Shīʿah, Sunnīs, and the Ḥashwiyyah nevertheless alleged omissions or changes in phrasing or sequence, while agreeing that no Muslim has claimed additions to the Qur’an. Their first argument rests on numerous reports in both traditions about missing sūrahs, verses, words, and letters, purportedly omitted in the collections under Abū Bakr and ʿUthmān. These claims are distinct from reports of differences in companions’ personal codices, in the Uthmanic copies sent to regions, in sūrah order, and in unusual readings. Their second argument says that fallible compilers could not be expected to preserve the text without deficiency. Their third invokes reports that Imām ʿAlī compiled and offered a codex after the Prophet’s death, reasoning that he would not have offered it had it been identical with Zayd b. Thābit’s codex. Their fourth invokes reports that this community will follow the Children of Israel, who altered their scripture.

The commentary first rejects using consensus as decisive proof here. Consensus is a juridical proof for those who accept it, and in belief produces at most conjecture, however many individual conjectures support it. For Sunnīs, it rests on the report that the community will not unanimously err; for Shīʿah, it has force insofar as it includes or reveals the infallible’s view. In either case, its authority presupposes the truth of prophethood, which depends upon the Qur’an’s remaining a decisive, guiding, miraculous divine proof. To establish that proof by a consensus whose authority itself rests on the Qur’an would be circular.

The reports alleged to establish distortion are isolated rather than tawātur, mutually divergent, and often weak or mursal; even reports with acceptable chains are vulnerable to fabrication or alterations in earlier written sources. Many do not actually establish textual corruption. They commonly quote wording as explanatory glosses on a verse, identify the occasion of revelation, state a particular application—such as an application concerning Imām ʿAlī and the Imāms—or include supplications to be said after recitation. Such material was mistakenly treated as omitted Qur’anic text. Variant wording may likewise explain the intended sense rather than constitute a different text. Other reports, including the varying alleged versions of the “verse of stoning” and expanded forms of Āyat al-Kursī, conflict with one another and should be set aside.

The prevalence of fabrication in hadith material about creation, prophets, ancient nations, Qur’anic exegesis, and early Islamic events makes alleged distortion reports especially unreliable, since enemies of religion had the strongest motive to undermine the Book on which prophethood and religion stand. Invented alleged sūrahs, such as Sūrah al-Khalʿ, Sūrah al-Ḥafd, and Sūrah al-Wilāyah, fail to resemble the Qur’an’s style and are exposed by comparison with it. Even a ṣaḥīḥ chain only excludes deliberate lying by the immediate transmitters; it does not exclude prior alteration of their source materials. More fundamentally, reports of corruption conflict not merely with the apparent force of (15:9) and (Fussilat:41-42), which by themselves would yield conjectural proof, but with the definite cumulative evidence of the Qur’an’s own harmonious, miraculous, coherent, and comprehensive reality.

It does not follow merely from the fallibility of compilers that distortion must have occurred. Such a possibility could be considered only if no contextual indications established the compilation’s fidelity. Nor does Imām ʿAlī’s presentation of his codex prove a difference in the substance of revelation. Its difference may have been in the order of sūrahs or verses. Had fundamental religious truths or verses specifically establishing his status been omitted, he would have argued against their omission; no such protest is reported. The suggestion that thousands of verses on walāyah disappeared is also implausible in view of the Prophet’s public teaching and dissemination of the Qur’an. Reports of enormous omissions are mursal or otherwise unsupported.

The Sunni notion that verses were forgotten and their recitation abrogated fares no better. If verses were removed because their rulings ceased, the continued presence of unpractised verses becomes problematic; those who affirm abrogation of recitation distinguish verses abrogated both in rule and recitation from verses whose recitation alone was abrogated, such as the supposed stoning verse. If forgotten verses lacked Qur’anic attributes, their removal would contradict “Indeed it is an august Book: falsehood cannot approach it, from before it nor from behind it” (Fussilat:41-42), and would undermine the Qur’an’s decisiveness, guidance, light, miraculous nature, and office as a Reminder. The unrestricted Qur’anic descriptions cannot be confined to the portion now extant while excluding allegedly forgotten verses.

Reports that this community will follow previous nations are widely transmitted, but they do not mean likeness in every respect. The likeness may concern division into sects, mutual accusations of unbelief, and prejudiced interpretation of one shared Qur’an through unreliable exegetical reports, not the existence of different Qur’anic texts. Thus the alleged parallels with the Children of Israel do not prove that the Qur’an was altered.

The commentary next surveys the reports on compilation. Tārīkh al-Ya’qūbī and Tārīkh Abū al-Fidāʾ report that, after reciters were killed at Yamāmah, ʿUmar urged Abū Bakr to collect the Qur’an from scattered written materials and the memories of men; the latter report ultimately draws on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī. Al-Bukhārī reports Zayd b. Thābit’s account that Abū Bakr commissioned him, despite his initial reluctance, to gather it from palm leaves, white stones, and people’s memories, and that the final verses of Sūrat al-Tawbah were found with Khuzayma al-Anṣārī. The sheets then remained with Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and Ḥafṣa. Other reports from Ibn Abī Dāwūd and al-Itqān say that ʿUmar and Zayd required two witnesses for verses, while the final verses of Barāʾah were admitted on the basis that the Prophet counted Abū Khuzaimah’s testimony as two; ʿUmar’s purported stoning verse was not recorded because he lacked a second witness.

Other transmitted accounts say that ʿUbayy b. Kaʿb supplied the final two verses of Barāʾah when the compilers thought the preceding verse was the end; that the Prophet died before the Qur’an was gathered in one document; and that Zayd and others had collected material during the Prophet’s lifetime. Reports variously name Ibn ʿUmar, several Anṣār, and Sālim, the freed slave of Abū Ḥudhaifah, as having compiled the Qur’an. Al-Mizan concludes that, at most, these reports show the gathering of revealed sūrahs and verses; they do not prove that their detailed current order, or any particular order, was already established. A single-volume official compilation after the Prophet’s death is indisputable.

The second official compilation under ʿUthmān was prompted by divergent manuscripts and readings. Al-Ya’qūbī reports that he organized copies, sent them to regions, and eliminated other copies, while Ibn Masʿūd resisted surrendering his manuscript. Al-Bukhārī reports that Ḥudhayfah, alarmed by regional differences in recitation, urged ʿUthmān to save the community from differing over the Book as Jews and Christians had done. ʿUthmān borrowed Ḥafṣa’s sheets, appointed Zayd b. Thābit, ʿAbdullāh b. al-Zubayr, Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ, and ʿAbdur Raḥmān b. Ḥārith b. Ḥishām to make copies, and instructed that disputes be written in the dialect of Quraysh. Zayd reports that a verse from Sūrat al-Aḥzāb was sought and found with Khuzaima b. Thābit al-Anṣārī before being included.

Further reports describe the compilers consulting those who had heard a disputed verse from the Prophet; a committee of Quraysh and Anṣār working under ʿUthmān; and ʿAlī’s reported approval that Muslims unite on one manuscript so as to avoid division. Al-Durr al-manthūr reports that Abū intervened to retain the wāw in “Wa alladhīna yakanizūna adh-dhahaba wal-fiḍḍah.” In a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUthmān explains that he joined al-Anfāl and Barāʾah without the basmalah and placed them among al-Sabʿ al-Ṭiwāl because of their similar subject matter, though the Prophet had not clarified whether they were one sūrah. The commentary infers that the first compilation apparently placed the seven long sūrahs in a different sequence, and that ʿUthmān later inserted al-Anfāl and Barāʾah between al-Aʿrāf and Yūnus.

These compilation reports are individual rather than tawātur reports, but strong circumstances support their broad purport: the Prophet disclosed all revelation and taught it; reciters preserved, taught, and publicly recited it; and the Qur’an never disappeared from the community even briefly before a consensual codex was produced. Numerous reports also describe the Prophet publicly reciting named sūrahs in obligatory and recommended prayers. A narration from ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ says that Gabriel instructed the Prophet to place “Indeed, Allah enjoins justice and kindness...” (al-Naḥl:90) at a specified place in its sūrah, and similar reports indicate that he directed the placement of some verses.

The text between the covers is therefore unquestionably God’s Word, with neither additions nor alterations. Yet, on the basis of compilation reports alone, the commentary says that possible omissions cannot be decisively denied, citing the recurrent reports of a stoning verse not included in the official text; nor do those reports demonstrate that it was abrogated in recitation. Personal codices of ʿAlī, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, and Ibn Masʿūd did not oppose the official text’s contents, apart from reports that Ibn Masʿūd excluded Sūrah al-Falaq and Sūrah al-Nās because he considered them protections sent to the Prophet for al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn. Other companions and the Imāms contested that view, and reports affirming the two sūrahs as Qur’an are tawātur. The decisive basis for the Qur’an’s authenticity remains its possession of the divinely stated attributes of clarification, resolution of disputes, dhikr, guidance, light, true knowledge, and miracle. These intrinsic qualities establish its divine origin without dependence on external tawātur, unlike ordinary books, letters, or sayings.

The arrangement of sūrahs, however, is attributed to the companions in the first and second compilations. Reports describe Imām ʿAlī’s codex as arranged according to revelation, and the codices of others, including Ibn Masʿūd, as having different orders. Claims that the present sūrah order is divinely prescribed and transmitted by tawātur are unsupported by the cited reports; accounts of the Qur’an’s descent from the Preserved Tablet to the nearest heaven do not establish that it was there arranged in the present muṣḥaf order.

Similarly, the location of verses separately revealed was not wholly free from the companions’ ijtihād. The report that Gabriel directed one specified verse’s placement cannot establish the placement of every scattered verse. Reports that the Prophet and believers recognized a sūrah’s conclusion when the Basmala was revealed indicate that revelation was arranged in its revealed order: Meccan verses in Meccan sūrahs and Medinan verses in Medinan sūrahs, except for one partly Meccan and partly Medinan sūrah. Yet many reports concerning occasions of revelation place Meccan verses in Medinan sūrahs and vice versa, or late verses in early sūrahs, such as the verses on ribā in al-Baqarah. This apparently resulted from companions’ ijtihād.

The majority’s claim that the present arrangement of all verses was prophetically prescribed is not established by consensus or tawātur. Reports concerning a few people who had compiled the Qur’an in the Prophet’s lifetime do not show that all Muslims knew every verse’s precise placement, especially when Zayd’s own reports show that he did not have every verse at hand. Nor do reports of the Prophet’s directing a particular placement prove a universal arrangement. Assertions that the Companions merely collected an already ordered text, or that the present order was fixed in the Preserved Tablet, lack evidence and conflict with the reports of the initial compilation and the descent of the Basmala.

Finally, Sunni reports about forgetting and abrogation are cited: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that the Prophet forgot by day what had been revealed at night; Abū Umāmah reports that a sūrah vanished from people’s memories and written locations overnight; Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ read “cause to be postponed” rather than “cause to be forgotten”; and Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that Gabriel presented the Qur’an twice to the Prophet in his final Ramaḍān, enabling Ibn Masʿūd to know what had been abrogated or changed. Such reports yield the theory that abrogation may concern rulings, recitation, or both. Al-Mizan maintains that the relevant verses do not concern removal from recitation, and that these reports contradict the explicit Qur’an; they should therefore be joined to reports alleging alteration and dismissed.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains shiyaʿ as the plural of shīʿah: a group united by a doctrine or school of thought. Although the sender is not named explicitly in “We sent,” the context makes clear that God sent the messengers; the emphasis is on prophethood itself rather than on particular prophets.

The verse shows that earlier communities, like later ones, rejected divine revelation, ridiculed their prophets, and committed evil. It consoles the Prophet: the mockery and rejection he faces are the established way of transgressors in every community, so he should not be distressed by their words. God has given him the Qur’an and will preserve it, while the prophets sent to former peoples likewise met their contemporaries’ derision.

verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains sulūk as passing something through or inserting it into something else. In both “We insert it” and “they do not have belief in it,” “it” most directly denotes the Reminder, the Qur’an. The Book is thus inserted into the hearts of evildoers, yet they persist in disbelieving in it and in the Prophet’s mission, following the pattern of earlier peoples who rejected the truth despite manifest proofs.

The commentary rejects the view that “it” means idolatry (shirk) or mockery and that the bā in lā yu’minūn bihi is causal. Its primary role is to make the verb transitive, not to mean that disbelief is caused by idolatry or mockery. Another interpretation—that the first pronoun denotes mockery and the second the Qur’an—is not problematic, despite the pronouns having different antecedents; but the context does not permit the second pronoun, in lā yu’minūn bihi, to mean mockery.

If the first pronoun is taken as God’s inspiring mockery, this does not mean that idolaters are compelled or initially predestined to mock. Such mockery follows their prior deep involvement in evil; God’s leading astray is figurative in this respect, and He does not misguide people from the outset. The verse is comparable to: “Thereby He leads many astray, and thereby He guides many; and He leads no one astray thereby except the transgressors” (al-Baqarah:26). Finally, the preferred meaning of “the way of life of the previous peoples” is the course earlier generations freely chose, not one God designated for them; this suits the verses’ rebuke of those who mock revelation and their consolation of the Prophet.

verses.14:
Al-Mizan explains urūj fī al-samā as ascent to the heavens and taskīr as the covering or overshadowing of sight. Opening “a gate of the sky” means providing a way into the higher world, the abode of angels, not opening a physical celestial ceiling with a two-leaved door.

This miracle is singled out because, in the disbelievers’ eyes, human ascent to heaven was the greatest of the miracles they demanded. Their requests culminated in ascent and in a book being brought down for them to read: “W e will never believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the ground, or you ascend into the sky. And even then, we will not believe your ascension until you bring down a book for us to read” (al-Isrā’:90-93). Ascending to heaven and exercising power over its affairs is akin to receiving such a book from it.

The heavens are the abode of angels, where divine judgments and decrees are issued, destinies are recorded, affairs begin, revelation descends, and human deeds ascend. Continuous ascent—not merely one ascent, as indicated by “they could go on ascending through it”—would give people repeated insight into these affairs, extraordinary events, revelation and prophethood, the call to righteousness, happiness and despair, and thus the truths underlying the mission.

Yet their corrupt hearts and entrenched doubts would cause them to misconstrue even this decisive disclosure. They would say that their sight had been clouded and that the Prophet had bewitched them, rather than accepting what they had witnessed.

verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains burūj as celestial “palaces,” namely the abodes of the sun and moon, metaphorically so called as palaces belong to kings. The pronouns in “adorned them” and “We have guarded them” refer to the sky, which God beautified for observers with stars of differing brightness and distance; this adornment also manifests His guardianship, as in “W e have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and guarded them” (Fussilat:12).

Istirāq al-samʿ means secretly obtaining information by listening, and here concerns devils attempting to overhear the angels’ discourse about unseen future matters. A shihāb, rendered “fame,” is a fiery spark; visible celestial bodies receive this name by resemblance, especially those star-like lights that dart rapidly across the sky and disappear. Thus, the sky is adorned and protected from malicious devils seeking to penetrate the unseen realm, save one who furtively overhears something and is then pursued by a piercing fame. The fuller meaning of this pursuit is deferred to the commentary on Sūrah al-Ṣāfāt.

verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains madd al-arḍ as extending the earth in length and breadth, making it fit for cultivation and habitation; were it covered only by high, deeply rooted mountains, it would not be suitable for life. Rawāsī means fixed mountains, cast upon the earth to stabilize it and prevent its shaking, as in “He cast into the earth frm mountains lest it shake with you” (al-Naḥl:15).

Mawzūn derives from wazn, originally weighing but extended to every kind of measurement, including nonphysical measures. It can also mean what accords with natural purpose and wisdom, without excess or deficiency. It has therefore been read as measurable minerals, plants with balanced systems, or every thing created with precision and knowledge. The commentary holds that “every kind of balanced thing,” rather than merely every balanced plant, includes what issues from the earth beyond plants. Yet anbatnā, “We grew,” specifically brings plants into view, while min indicates only a part. The verse thus refers to God’s producing all balanced entities, including plants and minerals affected by forces such as gravity, in quantities determined by divine wisdom; mawzūn may bear both its literal and figurative senses.

Maʿāyish denotes the means that sustain living beings, including food, drink, and other necessities. “For those whom you do not provide for” has been connected either to “for you,” under a grammatical analysis; to livelihoods for those humans maintain, such as servants and domestic animals; or to those whom humans do not maintain. Although these interpretations have difficulties, man can include non-rational beings—plants, animals, and others—because all seek sustenance. The Qur’an also uses expressions ordinarily applied to rational beings for non-rational things when rational attributes are ascribed to them. The verse consequently declares that God established on earth the means of human sustenance and those required by other beings.

verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that khazāʾin means treasuries or storehouses, while qadr denotes measure, decree, or ordainment. It rejects the restriction of “there is nothing” to plants, seeds, and fruits, and the identification of the divine treasures with measured rainfall. The wording is general, its context supplies no basis for such restriction, and rain is only one factor in plant growth rather than a plant’s treasure.

It also finds insufficient the view that the verse concerns only genera rather than individual things: on that account, all kinds belong to God, their existences, attributes, effects, and acts are known and finite, and they emerge only in decreed measure. But this reading unjustifiably narrows the verse, reduces qadr to numerical quantity, employs an unsupported metaphorical meaning, and gives no evident account of the plural khazāʾin. Qadr is closer in meaning to ḥadd, a limit, as indicated by verses such as “Certainly God has set a measure for everything” (al-Ṭalāq:3) and “Indeed We have created everything in a measure” (al-Qamar:49).

The commentary likewise presents a contemporary explanation: the treasures are the abundant, replenished elements and causal powers from which compounds, sustenance, and living things arise. Light, heat, winds, water, and elemental constituents are continually available; when plants and animals perish, their compounds decompose and return to their elements, allowing successors to arise. On this view, each thing has its own treasury, including its elements and causes, and only a limited quantity is released at any one time. This account is supported by natural evidence and Qur’anic verses concerning fertilizing winds, water, and the subjection of the sun, moon, and clouds. Yet, although sound in itself, it does not fully fit the present verse or the wider Qur’anic usage of qadr, including decreeing, proportioning, guiding, and the Night of Decree.

The verse instead concerns a deeper principle: all things manifest through qadr. “There is nothing” includes every thing, visible or unseen, both individuals such as Zayd and kinds such as humanity; only God, possession, and the treasures are excluded by the wording itself. Their “descent” is not spatial movement but creation, as in the sending down of cattle and iron. Since creation is inseparably accompanied by “a known measure,” every existent is confined by a predetermined measure.

This measure gives each thing its distinct identity, differentiating Zayd from other persons and from every other kind. Its faculties, effects, and acts are likewise proportioned and limited: sight, for example, operates only under particular conditions, times, places, objects, organs, and prerequisites; absolute sight would encompass every mode of seeing. Qadr therefore means the distinctive essence and manner of a thing’s creation. Because God gives each thing its creation and then guides it, its direction toward its existential end follows from the distinct attributes inseparable from its decreeing.

“Known measure” further shows that every thing’s destiny is determined and known before its finalized manifestation. God’s decree, in knowledge and will, precedes the actual thing, though in reality it is inseparable from it. Before descent into this world, things are with God as treasures, unquantified and unlimited; measurement accompanies their descent. Khazāʾin thus signifies a level beyond measurable and countable plurality, where the treasures are infinite, unified, and indistinguishable. Some treasures precede others, and descent may proceed through stages, each introducing a new decree.

Because these treasures are “with” God, they lie beyond the tangible, changing, perishing world: what is with God endures, whereas worldly things are transient and mutable. The verse is among the Qur’an’s profound utterances, and, for those unable to follow this fuller account, the commentary regards the third interpretation as the most reliable preliminary understanding. The subject of decree is to be treated further elsewhere, God willing.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains lawāqiḥ as fertilizing winds. Laqḥ, in the case of date palms, means placing the pollen of the male upon the female for fruit-bearing; botanical study likewise confirms male and female plants and the wind’s transport of pollen between them. “We send down water from the sky providing it for you to drink” refers to rain descending from clouds, from which Earth’s water primarily comes, contrary to the ancient belief that water was an incomplete sphere surrounding the earth as one of four elements.

The verse thus affirms plant duality and fertilization, and indicates that Earth’s stored waters ultimately become rain. In connection with the preceding statement that God sends things down in a known measure, it also points to the importance of measurement in plant growth. The Qur’an’s disclosure of these matters before their scientific discovery is deemed miraculous, or itself the miracle.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as an exclusive affirmation that all governance and management belong to God. The ordered signs previously mentioned—the heavens and stars, earth and mountains, measured growth, sustenance, fertilizing winds, and rain—belong to a divine system grounded in wisdom and knowledge; it is complete only with life, death, and resurrection. The verse therefore refutes those who suppose that some forms of life or death are not from God: He alone gives life and causes death.

“We are the inheritors” means that God remains after people have died and consumed the provisions granted them. He preceded them by giving them life from nonexistence, encompasses their affairs, causes their death, and inherits what was theirs after their passing.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan explains that, after displaying divine bounties and governance as proofs of God’s Oneness in lordship, the verse affirms His comprehensive knowledge of those who came earlier into existence and those who came later. Such knowledge is necessary to the ordered creation and governance, especially of those to whom He gives life and upon whom He decrees death. Interpretations that make the predecessors and successors those foremost in good deeds, battle ranks, or the rows of congregational prayer lack substantial support.

The commentary takes “and indeed it is your Lord who will resurrect them” as an exclusive assertion that God alone, as their Lord, will gather them on the Day of Resurrection. The issue is not merely who will perform an accepted gathering, but whether resurrection and gathering will occur at all. The shift from addressing the people to addressing the Prophet reflects that the Prophet already accepts this truth: from his perspective the discourse shifts from the first person plural to the third person, and from the people’s perspective from the second person to the third.

God’s being all-wise and all-knowing establishes the resurrection’s basis. Wisdom requires the accounting of deeds, reward for the virtuous, and punishment for wrongdoers, while His knowledge ensures that no one is wronged.

verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains ṣalṣāl as dry clay, named for the sound made by a dry object; al-Rāghib also reports an opinion connecting it with the foul smell of decayed clay. Ḥamʾah is foul-smelling black clay, and “aging mud” may denote clay that has undergone alteration. The verse concerns the first stages of the creation of the human species. In conjunction with “He commenced man’s creation from clay. Then He made his progeny from an extract of a base fluid” (al-Sajdah:7-8), it shows that humanity originates in the first human and shares one mode of creation.

Citing Majma’ al-bayyān, the commentary holds that the descriptions of Adam’s material do not conflict but name successive stages: dust became clay, the clay changed into limp, aging mud, and it was then left to dry into ṣalṣāl.

Al-Mizan explains that al-samūm is a hot, poisonous wind, and that jinn, whose name derives from concealment, are normally hidden from human senses. The Qur’an portrays them as beings with perception and free will, obligations, life, death, resurrection, and extraordinary swift acts. Although jānn has been variously identified as the jinn collectively, their father, Iblīs—as reported from Imām al-Ḥasan—his progeny, or a particular kind of jinn, most of these views lack conclusive support.

The Qur’anic contrast of insān with jānn presents humans and jinn as two distinct species, unrelated in their creation; comparison with usages pairing humans with jinn shows that jānn and jinn denote the same entity. The context and “He was one of the jinn, so he transgressed against his Lord’s command” (al-Kahf:50) establish that Iblīs was a jinn, so jānn here is either the whole class or a class within it. The verse concerns the jinn’s original creation, just as the preceding verse concerns humanity’s original creation. Though the Qur’an mentions Iblīs’s offspring and the mortality of jinn, it does not state whether their later reproduction is from fire or by what method.

“Earlier” is understood from the comparison of the two species to mean that jinn were created before humankind. Their creation from a piercing flame does not conflict with their creation from a flame of fire: the latter is a smoky flame, and together the verses indicate an initial piercing flame that ignited and became a smokeless flame of fire. Thus humanity began from dry clay formerly a malodorous liquid, and the jinn from such a piercing flame.

Al-Mizan explains that bashrah is the outer skin and admah what lies beneath it. Bashar denotes human beings because their skin is exposed rather than covered by wool, fur, or fluff; its singular and plural forms are alike, and the Qur’an uses it where human appearance is at issue.

“ When your Lord said to the angels” implies “Remember when your Lord said to the angels.” The shift from the preceding majestic plural, “We created,” to the third person is akin to the address concerning resurrection in (15:25) and relates to resurrection, everlasting felicity, and enduring wretchedness. The preceding plural is a plural of majesty, including the noble angels as executors of divine commands, not as partners in Adam’s creation. They receive the announcement of God’s will, and only after Adam is shaped and given the spirit are they commanded to prostrate.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan defines taṣwīyah as making a thing stable and proportionate, with every part in its proper place and condition; for the body, it is the exact ordering of its limbs and organs. The verse may describe the first human body’s gradual formation: khalq first assembled its parts, taṣwīyah arranged them properly, and nafkh followed with the spirit. This does not conflict with “He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be’, and he was” (Āl ʿImrān:59), for “Be” concerns the creation of the human spirit or soul rather than the physical body, as is also suggested by “Then We produced him as (yet) another creature” (al-Mu’minūn:14).

Nafkh, literally blowing air into a body, is here a metaphor for God’s originating the spirit and attaching it to the body; it does not mean that the spirit occupies the body as air occupies a vessel. The Qur’anic account of bodily development and its account of death show that the spirit is connected with the body without being an added bodily part: at death it departs, although nothing physical is removed. Thus the spirit subsists independently while attached to the body, and that attachment ends in death.

By calling it “My spirit,” God both honors the spirit and affirms His ownership of it. The angels are explicitly commanded to prostrate before Adam—possibly, to fall to the ground before him in prostration—thereby displaying humility before this new creation. The verse therefore means that once Adam’s body was completed and proportioned, and the noble spirit attributed to God was created and joined to it, the angels were to prostrate.
verses.30: Al-Mizan holds that the combined emphases ’ajma’ūn and kulluhum establish that every angel without exception prostrated before Adam; Iblīs alone refused. Yet Iblīs was not an angel, as “He was one of the jinn so he transgressed against his Lord’s command” (al-Kahf:50) confirms. The proposals that a class of angels was called jinn, or that jinn here means every “covered creation,” are untenable. Iblīs was commanded to prostrate despite not belonging to the angels.

verses.32: Al-Mizan explains mā laka as an interrogative expression meaning, in effect, “What is the matter with you?” The construction allā takūn omits a governing particle and asks why Iblīs was not among those who prostrated—namely, the angels. The verse therefore asks what prevented him from joining them.
verses.33: Al-Mizan notes that Iblīs’s wording, “I was not to prostrate” (lam akun li-asjuda), rather than a simple present or future refusal, portrays his refusal as intrinsic to his nature, as though it necessarily followed from what he was. It implicitly conveys the claim made explicitly elsewhere: “I am better than him: You created me from fire, and You created him from clay” (al-A’rāf:12).
verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains rajīm as one driven away, and la’n as being driven from mercy. Thus the curse until the Day of Retribution explains Iblīs’s being an outcast: he was expelled from the angels or from a divine station of nearness and special mercy. The same curse is explicitly attributed to God in “And indeed My curse will be on you till the Day of Retribution,” (Ṣād:78).

The general wording of the curse reflects Iblīs’s part in every act of disobedience through temptation or whispering: he is the root of sin, and the curse associated with sins ultimately traces back to him. When anyone other than God curses, it is a supplication that someone be removed from divine mercy; God alone effects that removal.

Majma’ al-bayyān observes that the definite “the curse” here and “My curse” in Sūrah Ṣād differ only with their surrounding phrasing, and concludes that the verse shows Iblīs was never a believer. The curse’s term until the Day of Retribution also shows that it concerns the spiritual injury produced by transgression in this world of action; that day is the realm of reckoning and just recompense. Its apparent sense is that the curse continues until that day and is followed by Iblīs’s punishment, not that retribution itself ends beforehand. The suggestion that the endpoint merely marks the furthest limit of creation is compared with “They shall remain in it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure” (Hūd:107). Treating this as a merely created curse that ceases on the Day of Judgment conflicts with the enduring divine act of distancing from mercy and ignores “And indeed My curse will be on you till the Day of Retribution” (Ṣād:78).

verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains indhār as granting respite. Although Iblīs was arrogant and disobedient, he addressed God as “my Lord” because he was supplicating and invoking God’s dominion and mercy. The fā’ introducing his request indicates that he sought respite in relation to all humanity, not Adam alone.

The commentary maintains that Adam represented humanity in the command of prostration. The angels’ prostration signified their humble service to humankind and their role in assisting human prosperity and perfection: they include the agents of life, death, sustenance, revelation, accompaniment, protection, and record-keeping. Iblīs’s refusal therefore arose from his unwillingness to humble himself before humanity or serve its perfection. By refusing, he separated himself from the angels and undertook opposition to humans throughout their earthly existence.

The curse imposed from his defiance until the Day of Judgment corresponds to the duration of humanity’s earthly life and precedes his stated intention to mislead all people. It reveals an animosity extending from Adam to his final descendant. Seemingly, Iblīs inferred from the curse that his fate was linked with humanity’s condition until its resurrection, and therefore requested postponement not merely until Adam’s death but until the resurrection of Adam’s descendants. Once respite was granted, he disclosed his purpose: “I will mislead them all, every one of them” (15:39).
verses.37:
Al-Mizan holds that God granted Iblīs the requested extension of life but rejected its requested endpoint. “The Day whose time is known” differs from “the Day they are resurrected” and must precede it; hence the unrestricted wording “You are one of the reprieved” (al-A’rāf:15) is qualified by this sūrah and Sūrah Ṣād. Qur’anic passages clarify one another in this manner.

The known Day is a time fixed in God’s knowledge, as in “We only send it down in a known measure” (15:21). The verse does not establish whether Iblīs knows that time. The claim that God concealed it from Iblīs lest disclosure encourage further evil is unsupported. Iblīs’s promise to mislead all humans indicates that he understood the Day as the last day during which people susceptible to his deception remain on earth.

A view attributed to Ibn ‘Abbās and accepted by many identifies it with the first trumpet-blast, when all creatures die; reports place forty or four hundred years between it and the resurrection blast. This view rests on the premise that Iblīs endures as long as religious obligation, and thus the possibility of sin, remains. Al-Mizan rejects that premise: the texts establish only that Iblīs exists wherever sin and misguidance exist, not that he must exist wherever obligation exists.

Reason and scripture instead indicate that human felicity will ultimately prevail: society will incline to righteousness, God alone will be worshipped, and disbelief, immorality, inner disease, and whispering will disappear. “It is My servants who are righteous who will inherit the earth” (al-Anbiyā’:105). The known Day is therefore the day on which God rectifies human society, uproots corruption, and establishes His worship, rather than the day when all creation perishes at the first trumpet.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan holds that God granted Iblīs the requested extension of life but rejected its requested endpoint. “The Day whose time is known” differs from “the Day they are resurrected” and must precede it; hence the unrestricted wording “You are one of the reprieved” (al-A’rāf:15) is qualified by this sūrah and Sūrah Ṣād. Qur’anic passages clarify one another in this manner.

The known Day is a time fixed in God’s knowledge, as in “We only send it down in a known measure” (15:21). The verse does not establish whether Iblīs knows that time. Iblīs’s promise to mislead all humans indicates that he understood the Day as the last day during which people susceptible to his deception remain on earth.

verses.39:
Al-Mizan takes the bā’ in bi-mā aghwaytanī, “because You misled me,” as causal, not as an oath. Iblīs declares that, because of his own misguidance, he will beguile humanity and maintain it in sin. His attribution of misguidance to God does not mean that God initially misled him when he refused to prostrate. Rather, he refers to the curse already imposed on him: his exclusion from mercy and happiness, brought about by his own inward deception. Misguidance attributed to God is thus figurative and retributive, not initial, as in “He misguides many by it and guides many by it. But He only misguides the deviators” (al-Baqarah:26). Iblīs misleads others by extending to them the effects of his own estrangement from divine mercy.

The commentary rejects both the determinist inference that this proves good and evil alike originate from God in the same way and the attempts to evade the issue by redefining “misled” as making Iblīs despair, diverting him from Paradise, or merely commanding him to prostrate. It also rejects accounts that make his reprieve an arbitrary divine permission to mislead or merely a means to magnify believers’ reward. They overlook that felicity and misery, reward and punishment, are founded upon trial: people stand between calls to good and calls to evil, and their outcomes follow their choices. Without the angelic or divine call toward good and Iblīs’s call toward evil, trial would be meaningless.

God’s respite of Iblīs until the fixed Day is balanced by angelic guidance for as long as the world lasts. Humanity is also given love of faith, a natural inclination to Tawḥīd, discernment of immorality and piety, divine light for believers, and divine aid. People begin neither destined for bliss nor misery, but before two paths: angelic obedience and Iblīs’s rebellion. Their chosen path and its companions draw them toward its final abode, Paradise or Hell. Iblīs’s reprieve is therefore neither arbitrary nor contrary to causality; it enables the trial in which he and the angels play opposing roles.

“I will beguile them with the things upon the earth” may mean making falsehood generally, or disobedience specifically, attractive. It concerns Adam and his descendants and identifies the world’s allure as the cause whose result is misguidance. Al-Mizan reaffirms that Adam’s eating from the tree followed Iblīs’s whispering but was a departure from divine counsel, not a violation of a binding command, and so did not impair Adam’s infallibility. Iblīs could not deceive Adam and his wife in the Garden; he could only induce their departure to earth, where their procreation gave him the occasion to mislead them and their descendants.

The exception is the mukhlasūn, those whom God has made sincere after their own sincere devotion to Him. Chosen for exclusive devotion, they have no attachment or ownership in action or heart besides God, and Iblīs’s temptations only intensify their remembrance of Him. The exception concerns being successfully misled, not Iblīs’s attempt to beautify evil, which he makes toward all. The ordering “Your servants” and then “made sincere” further shows that true servitude consists in God’s exclusive possession of the servant: one must claim no ownership of one’s being, attributes, effects, or acts, for mulk belongs solely to God.

verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains “This is a Straight Path to Me” as an assertion that every affair falls under God’s lordship and decree and nothing is independent of Him. The path is directly bound to Him, its beginning and end, just as a traveller’s route itself dictates the preparations required for the journey.

The statement answers Iblīs’s boast that he will mislead almost all humanity while exempting the sincere. That boast assumes an autonomy from God’s decree in the affairs of human creation, vicegerency, and servitude. God’s answer is that He alone governs and judges this affair: Iblīs can mislead only by God’s permission and can be prevented only by His will; his power is a grant, not an independent possession. Its specific limitation follows: “You have no authority over any of My servants except for the misled who follow you” (15:42).
verses.42:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse concerns misguidance, an affair governed exclusively by God. “My servants” means Adam and all his descendants, not only the made-sincere. Iblīs has no autonomous dominion over them; his authority is confined to those who have gone astray, follow him, and entrust their guidance to him.

The verse refutes Iblīs’s claim in three respects. First, he treated God’s servants as only the sincere and presumed authority over everyone else; God declares all humanity His servants and limits Iblīs to one category among them. Second, Iblīs claimed an independent resolve to mislead in defiance of God, whereas his influence occurs only by divine decree. His authority reaches those who choose to follow him because of their own defective choice, and neither he nor the sincere he excluded ever stands outside God’s judgment. This accords with Tawḥīd: all affirmation and negation prevail only by God’s command.

Third, Iblīs’s influence is not an initial power exercised against persons with no prior disposition to error. It is a retributive authority following their inclination toward his deception. There is thus a distinction between initial ghawāyah, arising from human wrongdoing and choice, and subsequent ighwā’, effected by Iblīs as divine requital. If he initially misled the undeserving, blame would rest on him rather than the sinner; instead, “I had not authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me. Do not, therefore, blame me but blame yourselves” (14:22). Iblīs remains blameworthy for his own evil choice and for misleading, while the authority granted him after his refusal to prostrate does not remove human responsibility.

Accordingly, the exception is continuous, not disjointed: “from the misled” identifies the followers excepted from the generality of God’s servants. Interpretations restricting “My servants” to the sincere, or making the exception disjointed to deny Iblīs any divinely granted authority, weaken the confrontational force of God’s reply and merely repeat Iblīs’s claim. The fact that the misled may outnumber the sincere does not prevent the exception, because it distinguishes categories, not numerical units. Humanity includes the sincere, those not accountable or weak in faith, and those who follow Iblīs; only the last are named in the exception. His authority is consequential rather than inherent, and divinely decreed while still following their voluntary allegiance, as supported by “It has been decreed upon him that whoever turns to him, he will mislead them” (al-Hajj:4).

“Hell is the tryst of them all” identifies Hell as the promised meeting-place where punishment of Iblīs’s astray followers is fulfilled. It confirms that their punishment and Iblīs’s derivative authority return to God’s power; the verse speaks specifically of their fate, not of Iblīs’s own punishment, which is addressed differently elsewhere.

verses.44:
Al-Mizan says that the Qur’an does not explicitly determine whether Hell’s seven gates are physical entrances or degrees and kinds of punishment. Since “gates” can denote categories, means, or ways leading to something, and since other verses mention Hell’s gates and its lowest reach, the more plausible meaning is categories or levels of punishment rather than entrances to one enclosure.

“To each gate belongs a separate portion” indicates that a specified, distinct group is allotted to each gate. Hence Hell’s seven gates signify seven categories of punishment, corresponding to categories of the sins that lead to it and the paths and motives leading to those sins. The transmitted traditions support this general meaning.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that the Godwary are settled amid Gardens and Springs and are told to enter in peace and safety, secure from every harm and evil. After declaring Hell for Iblīs’s astray followers, God states Paradise for the righteous. Taqwā is avoidance of what God has forbidden, and the muttaqūn are therefore broader than the mukhlasūn, the made-sincere.

The view that the Godwary here are identical with the made-sincere rests on wrongly restricting “My servants” in (15:42) to that group. Since God’s servants comprise all humanity and only the astray followers are excepted, the passage assigns Hell to the astray and Paradise to the pious believers. It does not decide the fate of those incapable of accountability or of grave sinners who die unrepentant; the latter’s final outcome depends on possible intercession. The Godwary promised Paradise are consequently believers in whom piety is established, not merely the specially sincere.

Al-Mizan rejects Imām al-Rāzī’s reported interpretation that al-Muttaqīn includes everyone who abstains from shirk, even one who commits all other major sins or omits obligations. Al-Rāzī argues that a person may be called muttaqī after a single act of taqwā, that the community agrees faith is required, and that no further qualification should be imposed; he therefore extends the promise to all who profess, “There is no god but God, Muḥammad is the Messenger of God,” including sinners.

The commentary responds that Qur’anic usage does not call a person muttaqī merely for one isolated abstention. Like “believer,” “doer of good,” “obedient,” “sincere,” and “patient,” such descriptions require a rooted and continuing quality. The Qur’an repeatedly promises Paradise to the muttaqūn and depicts them as avoiding prohibitions. Otherwise the same reasoning would make persons who commit a single wrong firmly “wrongdoers,” “corrupt,” or “misguided,” producing incoherence; verses on repentance, intercession, and major sins also qualify isolated acts. An unqualified wording is evidence only where no valid contextual specification exists, while many Qur’anic verses specify the scope here. The verse therefore promises enduring happiness and Paradise to those in whom taqwā—abstention from what God has forbidden—is established. This differs from the Qur’an and Sunnah’s teaching that professing Tawḥīd prevents everlasting residence in Hell and guarantees eventual entry into Paradise.

verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains al-ghill as rancor or ill-will, possibly including envy that impels harm; al-surur are couches, and al-naṣb is hardship caused by external factors. The verses select blessings of Paradise to show complete peace and security. Its inhabitants are safe from themselves because God removes rancor from their hearts; they sit as brothers facing one another. They are also safe from all external hardship and from expulsion by their Lord. Thus neither misery nor weakness reaches them from themselves, creation, or God.

The commentary then gathers ten foundational decrees issued at the beginning of human history. Iblīs was expelled and cursed until the Day of Reckoning; he was reprieved until the known Day; and his authority was denied over God’s servants except the astray followers. Adam and those with him were sent down as enemies, given earthly residence and enjoyment for a time. Finally, guidance was promised from God: those who follow it have neither fear nor sorrow, while those who disbelieve and deny the signs are the everlasting companions of the Fire. Other subsidiary decrees follow from these foundations.

verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Ḍayf, originally a verbal noun, can designate either one guest or many and is most eloquently left without dual or plural marking. Abraham’s “guests” were honored angels appearing as guests, sent both to announce a son and to destroy Lot’s people.

Their plural speech identifies them as angels, and their greeting, salāman, conveys respect. Abraham feared them only after offering them a roasted calf and seeing that they did not eat. They reassured him that they were messengers from his Lord and brought news of a knowledgeable son, that is, a young son endowed with wisdom. This may refer to divine knowledge and revelation bestowed upon the child.

verses.58:

verses.63:
Al-Mizan explains that what Lot’s people had doubted was the punishment with which Lot warned them. The angels’ statement that they brought “the truth” most likely means that they brought the just, irrevocable decision concerning those people, rather than merely a punishment free of doubt.

The narrative deliberately departs from the events’ natural sequence. Its four sections are: the messengers’ arrival at Lot’s house; the city people’s rejoicing arrival; the angels’ announcement of the punishment and command to depart; and the Cry. The third section is placed between the first and second so that the people’s bewilderment in drunkenness is joined directly to the Cry at sunrise. This highlights the suddenness of the overwhelming punishment that came while they were heedless and secure, deepening its shock, regret, and pain. The analogous juxtaposition of the People of the Rock’s security with the Cry at dawn serves the same purpose: clarifying that God’s punishment is painful.

verses.65: Al-Mizan explains that Isrâ is travel by night, while a watch of the night is a portion of it. Lot was commanded, once the irrevocable decree of punishment was set in motion, to lead his family out at night from behind, so that none would lag or be left behind, and none should look back. They were to proceed as commanded, under divine guidance and a directing leader.
verses.66: Al-Mizan explains that qaḍāʾ, the divine decree or matter, is implicit in the act of revelation. Here the “matter” is the command of punishment, and the demonstrative dhālika underscores its gravity: God revealed to Lot His momentous decree that this people would be wholly cut off by dawn, including what might remain of their offspring, structures, and deeds. It is also possible to understand the wording simply as the revelation of God’s judgment.

verses.80:
Al-Mizan identifies the people of al-Ḥijr as the Thamūd, the people of Prophet Ṣāliḥ, and al-Ḥijr as their town. Though they denied Ṣāliḥ alone, the Qur’an calls them deniers of the messengers because all prophetic calls are essentially one, so rejecting one prophet is rejecting them all.

The Signs they disregarded apparently refer primarily to the she-camel, its drinking, and the events leading to their annihilation; they may instead be Ṣāliḥ’s divinely given teachings, or both teachings and the miraculous sign. Their rock-hewn dwellings in valleys and caves gave them a supposed security against earthly and heavenly calamities. Yet the Cry of punishment seized and destroyed them at dawn, showing the connection between their presumed safety and the painful punishment. Their earnings—the deeds they thought would secure their well-being—did not avail them.

verses.85:
Al-Mizan interprets “with the Truth” (bi al-ḥaqq) as meaning that creation is inseparably joined to truth and ordered toward an ultimate return to God. The particle ba denotes companionship or purpose, not causality. Since creation has this end, it is not futile play; the mention that the Hour is bound to come confirms that “the Truth” is contrasted with vain play.

The commentary rejects the claim that al-ḥaqq means justice and fairness, so that creation exists solely because of requital on the Day of Judgment: neither language nor the verse supports this. It also rejects the view that al-ḥaqq means wisdom, that the first clause concerns worldly punishment, and that the coming Hour concerns punishment in the hereafter. This improperly makes the verse mean that wisdom requires the destruction of corrupt people in this world and again at the Hour.

Al-Mizan also rejects both determinism (Jabr) and delegation (Tafwīḍ). Determinists argue that servants’ acts are created by God because they belong to what exists between heaven and earth; proponents of delegation argue that sins, being falsehood (bāṭil), cannot be created by God “with the Truth” (bi al-ḥaqq). But the act itself is one existent reality: obedience or disobedience, like lawful marriage and adultery or lawful and unlawful acquisition of wealth, differs only by conformity or contradiction to the command. Contradiction, immorality, and disobedience are non-existential aspects. Thus, creating an act in its existent aspect neither creates falsehood nor attributes its evil to God. Moral attribution belongs to the human being whose act depends upon the relevant causes, not to the Creator who created and enabled him, just as colour is attributed to the body in which it appears rather than to its creator.

Citing al-Rāghib, the commentary explains Ṣafḥ as a more expressive overlooking than mere forgiveness: one turns away gracefully from an offence and leaves the grievance behind. Therefore, because creation is by truth and an inescapable Day of Judgment will hold everyone accountable, the Prophet is commanded not to be troubled by their disbelief and mockery, but to forgive without reproach or disputation. “Indeed your Lord is the All-creator, the All-knowing” grounds this command: He created both parties, knows their states, and they cannot evade the coming Day. These verses console the Prophet against his people’s harm, insults, and derision so that he may fulfill the chapter’s central command: “So proclaim what you have been commanded.”

Al-Mizan holds that “the seven oft-repeated” (sabʿan min al-mathānī) is Sūrah al-Hamd (al-Fatiha), as numerous traditions from the Prophet and the Imāms of the Ahl al-Bayt explain. It dismisses the identifications with the long chapters, the seven chapters beginning with ḥā and mīm, or seven scrolls given to prophets, since neither the Qur’an nor tradition supports them.

God knows best, but min is apparently partitive: all Qur’anic verses are called “oft-repeated” in “A Book consistent in its frequent repetitions. The skins of those who fear their Lord tremble at it…,” (al-Zumar:23), and al-Hamd is therefore some, rather than the whole, of that category. Mathānī apparently is the plural of mathnīya, derived from bending, folding, or repeating. Verses are so called because some clarify, confirm, speak of, and bear witness to others; alternatively, it may be the plural of muthannā, denoting recurrence and likewise indicating that verses explain one another.

The commentary sets aside explanations based on repeated meanings or words, al-Fātiḥa’s recurrence in prayer, its alleged double revelation, its praise of God, or its being reserved for this Ummah. The verse magnifies both al-Fātiḥa and the Qur’an: the Qur’an is explicitly described as great, while al-Fātiḥa’s bare designation as “Seven,” joined to the Great Qur’an of which it is part, itself indicates its lofty worth. In this context of gratitude and graceful forbearance, this immense gift of truths leading, by God’s permission, to perfection and happiness directs the Prophet to attend to his Lord and obey Him.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as an elaboration of the command to practice graceful forbearance, through two prohibitions and two positive commands. “Do not extend your glance” warns the Prophet not to turn from gratitude for the manifest and hidden blessings God has given him toward the worldly luxuries granted to particular groups of disbelievers. Although some take it to mean prolonged looking, its real object is desire, inclination, and emotional attachment to their wealth, power, and standing; indeed, the prohibition concerns looking at such things, not merely lingering over them.

“Do not grieve for them” concerns their persistence in denial, mockery, and refusal to believe. “Lower your wing to the faithful” means humility and gentleness, like a bird lowering its wing over its young. More particularly in this context, it means patiently embracing believers, nurturing and training them in divine manners, and remaining close to them without abandoning them: “Content yourself with the company of those who supplicate their Lord morning and evening, desiring His Face, and do not lose sight of them, desiring the glitter of the life of this world” (al-Kahf:28). “I am indeed a manifest warner” limits the Prophet’s role to plainly warning of God’s coming punishment and clarifying what requires clarification.

Together, detachment from their worldly possessions, refusal to grieve over their unbelief and derision, humble care for believers, and affirmation of his office as a clear warner constitute the graceful forbearance required of the Prophet. Consequently, Al-Mizan rejects the claim that this forbearance was abrogated by the ‘Verse of the Sword’: the enduring instruction to turn away graciously includes the command not to direct one’s eyes longingly toward what they possess.

Al-Mizan explains “the dividers” (muqtasimūn) as those who “reduced the Qur’an into pieces”: the wording warns that punishment will be sent upon the addressees just as it was sent upon those dividers. Based on narrations, they were disbelievers of Quraysh in the early Prophetic mission who fractured the Qur’an by calling it magic, ancient legends, and fabrication, and who positioned themselves on Mecca’s roads during pilgrimage to turn arrivals away from the Prophet.

The commentary rejects the alternative that the verse means the Qur’an was revealed to Jews and Christians who accepted some of it and rejected other parts. The sūrah is Meccan and from the early mission, before the particular Jewish and Christian opposition invoked by that reading; its context therefore supports the Quraysh interpretation. It likewise rejects the claim that they were called dividers because they distinguished among prophets and scriptures, because the following verse specifically defines them as those who divided the Qur’an itself.

Apparently, then, the verses concern an early group that sought to extinguish the Qur’an’s light and divert people from God’s path by fragmenting it. God sent punishment upon them and destroyed them, while declaring that all of them will be questioned concerning what they used to do.

Al-Mizan explains ṣadaʿa bi al-ḥaqq as openly proclaiming the truth. These verses extend the preceding discourse and express the chapter’s central purpose: after commanding the Prophet to turn away graciously and warning of the punishment sent upon the dividers, God commands him to make the call and the truth public.

“Indeed We will suffice you against the deriders” supplies the reason for proclaiming the message and turning away from the polytheists. The deriders are apparently the same dividers previously mentioned: God will suffice the Prophet against them by punishing them. They are those who associate another god with Allah, and soon they will know.

verses.97: Al-Mizan says that the verse returns to the Prophet’s sorrow and inward distress caused by the mockers’ words in order to comfort him, console him, and strengthen his spirit. The Qur’an frequently addresses this matter, especially in Meccan chapters, because of its profound effect on him.
verses.98:
Al-Mizan explains that glorification, praise, prostration, and continual worship are commanded to relieve the Prophet’s distress at what the mockers say. They provide solace in adversity and entail perseverance in devotion, in harmony with “Take recourse in patience and prayer” (al-Baqarah:153). “Those who prostrate” means those who pray, prayer being named after its noblest part. Glorification and praise may mean verbal utterances such as “Glory be to God” and “Praise be to God”; if prayer in the cited verse means turning devoutly to God, they may instead, or together with prostration, carry their full linguistic sense of exalting God above their attributions, praising His blessings, and expressing utter submission.

“Worship your Lord until certainty comes to you” may explain the preceding commands if it is simply an order to worship. More apparently, in the context of forbearance and turning away, it commands a continuing path of servitude, obedience, and fulfillment of its duties. “Certainty” means the arrival of the appointed time—death—when the unseen becomes manifest and what was reported is directly witnessed. The command therefore is to remain patient in obedience, avoid disobedience, bear what they say, and persist until death, when the reality of God’s requital of them and reward according to deeds will be seen.

The wording also portrays certainty as something one will eventually attain: the afterlife, where there is universal certainty concerning what lay beyond the unseen veil. This is distinct from the certainty of belief that reflection or devotion may yield. Al-Mizan thus rejects the claim that religious duties cease when someone attains certainty. The verse addresses the Prophet, though the Qur’an describes him as possessing firm conviction, insight, proof from his Lord, infallibility, and divine guidance; moreover, the verse itself identifies certainty with death.
